title: Patton's men break into Metz
pull: The fortress city that had never been stormed

facts.text: On 18 November 1944, troops of the US Third Army closed on Metz, an old fortress city in Lorraine ringed by forts. The 5th Infantry Division pushed in from the south while the 95th Infantry Division came from the north and west.
Men of the 5th Division's 10th and 11th Infantry Regiments crossed the Metz city limits on 18 November. That same day, Army Signal Corps cameramen filmed P-47 Thunderbolts dive bombing the city.

Early on 18 November the Germans blew the bridges over the Moselle west of the city. One bridge went up while a patrol of the 378th Infantry was crossing it: eight men on the bridge were killed and five who had already crossed were cut off, though they were later rescued.

On 19 November the 377th and 378th Infantry and the 95th Division's Task Force Bacon all entered Metz proper. That morning the two divisions linked up inside the ring, and other 5th Division troops met the 90th Division east of the city, closing the trap.

The German army in the field had pulled back east and left the Metz garrison to its fate. There was no real house to house battle: most Germans outside the forts fired a few shots and then walked into the American lines with their hands up.

French resistance fighters of the FFI and two French intelligence networks, Mithridate and Navarre, helped the Americans. Signal Corps film from inside Metz on 19 November shows German prisoners under FFI guard.
Fighting in the city formally ended on the afternoon of 22 November 1944. The city of Metz dates the last shots to 1 p.m. that day.

The outer forts held out. General Walton Walker forbade direct assaults on them to save artillery shells, so they were left to starve. The last, Fort Jeanne d'Arc, did not surrender until 13 December 1944.

Time magazine wrote that week that Metz had never before been taken by storm. Attila's Huns destroyed it in 451, the magazine noted, but no Roman legions were there to defend it. In 1870 the fortress fell to the Prussians only after a long siege, not an assault.
German sources later put their losses in the defense of the city itself at about 400 dead and 2,200 wounded.
For France, the liberation of Metz ended four years of German annexation of the city.

photoNote: German soldiers taken prisoner in Metz walk through a cobbled street on their way to a collecting point, past civilians (a boy in front) and two Americans on a truck, one in a US helmet. US Army Air Forces photo, NARA 342-FH-3A17756 (USAF A55138AC), naId 204893546, use Unrestricted, US government work, public domain. Exact day not recorded: taken between the entry (18 to 19 November) and the formal end on 22 November 1944; negative received 2 December 1944. Cropped from the print mount, 1920 x 1505, grayscale. Frame on the boy and the column; some prisoners shield their faces. Alternatives: the 18 November Cole photo of 5th Division men entering Metz (Commons File:Metz1944-1.jpg, only 748 px) and the courtyard of prisoners, NARA 204893540.
photoCredit: German prisoners march through the streets of Metz, France, November 1944. US Army Air Forces photo, NARA 342-FH-3A17756, public domain.

declassified.fact: The German commander of Metz, Generalleutnant Heinrich Kittel, had been fighting in the line himself. On 21 November a patrol of the 95th Division found him in an underground field hospital, badly wounded and under morphine.

film.shot_notes: Signal Corps reel, silent, 9 min 27 s. 00:00 to 04:12: other stories (a 4.2 inch mortar crew in Luxembourg, 19 Nov; infantry in villages), not used. NOON: LIB 784, 'Capture of Metz', 18 Nov 1944, 04:16 to 06:04: long shots across the plain to Metz as P-47s dive bomb it, bomb bursts and smoke on the skyline (04:56 to 05:24 strongest), then infantry moving past houses and soldiers at a doorway (05:28 to 06:04). Open on a bomb burst. 7 P.M. SECOND CUT: LIB 785, 'Inside Metz', 19 Nov 1944, 06:16 to 09:12: shells exploding over the city (06:16 to 07:16), infantry running along a street past a tank (07:20), soldiers and civilians before a large barracks, a group of German prisoners under FFI guard (07:36 to 07:52), infantry dashing along streets and doorways (08:56 to 09:12). Open on infantry running at about 07:20. No shot of the noon stretch appears in it.
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (Army Signal Corps, NARA Record Group 111). NARA use status is 'Restricted, Possibly', the routine flag on 111-ADC reels; Signal Corps combat film is a U.S. government work.
film.date_note: Noon stretch filmed on the day, 18 Nov 1944. The 7 p.m. second cut is from inside Metz on 19 Nov 1944, the next day; its caption should say so.

video.note: U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2717 (NARA 16521), story LIB 784, 'Capture of Metz', 18 November 1944, silent. U.S. government work, public domain. Clip from the research copy footage/1944-11-18-metz-reel.mp4 (pillarbox cropped): 5:34.5 to 5:39.5 infantry with rifles move along a wall to a doorway; 4:38.5 to 4:43.5 bomb bursts on the plain before Metz as P-47s attack; 5:28 to 5:31 an antitank gun and a jeep in a village street; 5:54.6 to 5:57.4 a soldier with a rifle at a gateway. The 'Inside Metz' stretch (6:16 on, 19 Nov) is left for the 7 p.m. second cut.
video.hook: That morning the Germans blew the bridges.

kit.filmCaption:
Army cameramen outside Metz filmed the city under attack from the air on 18 November 1944.

Bombs from diving P-47 Thunderbolts burst on the plain before the city, infantry of the US Third Army edge along a wall toward a doorway, and a soldier keeps watch at a gateway. Real U.S. Army Signal Corps film, shot the day American troops crossed the city limits.

kit_b.filmCaption:
Inside Metz on 19 November 1944, one day after the first Americans got into the city. Infantry run along a street past an American gun, German prisoners wait under guard by French resistance fighters, and riflemen dash down a tree lined avenue.

Filmed by a U.S. Army Signal Corps crew. The original is silent.
